source_refs.note: Exercise 11.2, Question 2 (book page 211): two pairs of graphs on the same axes, parts (i)-(ii). Answer key PDF 309 gives small graphs only; ours are plotted from the functions. Solution book PDF 1015-1019.

blocks.prompt: 2 (i) On the same axes and to the same scale, draw the graphs of the following functions for their complete period: \(y = \sin x\) and \(y = \sin 2x\).
blocks.explanation:
Two sine curves on one graph so that we can compare them: same height, different speed.
Plan: one table for \(0 \le x \le 2\pi\) with both functions, plot both, and note where they meet.
steps:
Given: \(y = \sin x\) and \(y = \sin 2x\).
To find / draw: both graphs on the same axes for a complete period.
Method: \(\sin x\) has period \(2\pi\) and \(\sin 2x\) has period \(\pi\), so the interval \([0, 2\pi]\) holds one complete period of the first and two of the second. One table with both rows, one pair of axes, one scale.

Amplitudes and periods
\[\sin x:\ \text{amplitude } 1,\ \text{period } 2\pi\]
\[\sin 2x:\ \text{amplitude } 1,\ \text{period } \pi\]
Why: the 2 inside halves the period but does not change the height.

Table of values (shown below the answer)
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}:\ \sin x \approx 0.71,\ \sin 2x = 1\]
\[x = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}:\ \sin x \approx 0.71,\ \sin 2x = -1\]
Why: steps of \(\pi/4\) are a quarter period of \(\sin 2x\), so all its peaks and zeros are in the table.

Plot both curves
\(y = \sin x\): up to \(1\) at \(\pi/2\), down to \(-1\) at \(3\pi/2\), one cycle. \(y = \sin 2x\): up to \(1\) at \(\pi/4\) and \(5\pi/4\), down to \(-1\) at \(3\pi/4\) and \(7\pi/4\), two cycles.
Why: drawing both on one grid shows that sin 2x repeats twice as fast.

Where the curves meet
\[\sin 2x = \sin x\]
\[2\sin x\cos x - \sin x = 0\]
\[\sin x\,(2\cos x - 1) = 0\]
\[x = 0,\ \dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ 2\pi\]
Why: \(\sin x = 0\) gives \(0, \pi, 2\pi\); \(\cos x = 1/2\) gives \(\pi/3, 5\pi/3\). These are the crossing points visible on the graph.

Check
\[\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \approx 0.87\]
Why: at \(x = \pi/3\) both curves have height \(0.87\), so they really cross there.
blocks.final_answer: On \([0, 2\pi]\): \(y = \sin x\) makes one cycle (period \(2\pi\)) and \(y = \sin 2x\) makes two (period \(\pi\)), both of amplitude 1; the curves meet at \(x = 0, \pi/3, \pi, 5\pi/3, 2\pi\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) On the same axes and to the same scale, draw the graphs of the following functions for their complete period: \(y = \cos x\) and \(y = \cos 2x\).
blocks.explanation:
Two cosine curves on one graph: same height, \(\cos 2x\) twice as fast.
Plan: one table for \(0 \le x \le 2\pi\), plot both curves, find where they meet.
steps:
Given: \(y = \cos x\) and \(y = \cos 2x\).
To find / draw: both graphs on the same axes for a complete period.
Method: \(\cos x\) has period \(2\pi\) and \(\cos 2x\) has period \(\pi\); on \([0, 2\pi]\) the first makes one cycle and the second two. One table, one pair of axes, one scale.

Amplitudes and periods
\[\cos x:\ \text{amplitude } 1,\ \text{period } 2\pi\]
\[\cos 2x:\ \text{amplitude } 1,\ \text{period } \pi\]
Why: the 2 inside the angle changes only the period.

Table of values
\[x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}:\ \cos x = 0,\ \cos 2x = -1\]
\[x = \pi:\ \cos x = -1,\ \cos 2x = 1\]
Why: steps of \(\pi/4\) catch every peak and zero of \(\cos 2x\).

Plot both curves
\(y = \cos x\): from \(1\) at \(0\) down to \(-1\) at \(\pi\) and back to \(1\) at \(2\pi\). \(y = \cos 2x\): \(1\) at \(0, \pi, 2\pi\) and \(-1\) at \(\pi/2, 3\pi/2\).
Why: both start at their maximum 1, as every cosine curve does.

Where the curves meet
\[\cos 2x = \cos x\]
\[2\cos^2 x - \cos x - 1 = 0\]
\[(\cos x - 1)(2\cos x + 1) = 0\]
\[x = 0,\ \dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ 2\pi\]
Why: \(\cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x - 1\); \(\cos x = 1\) gives \(0, 2\pi\) and \(\cos x = -1/2\) gives \(2\pi/3, 4\pi/3\).

Check
\[\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = -\dfrac12,\ \cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = -\dfrac12\]
Why: at \(x = 2\pi/3\) both curves are at height \(-0.5\).
blocks.final_answer: On \([0, 2\pi]\): \(y = \cos x\) makes one cycle (period \(2\pi\)) and \(y = \cos 2x\) makes two (period \(\pi\)), both of amplitude 1; the curves meet at \(x = 0, 2\pi/3, 4\pi/3, 2\pi\).
